Concept briefDesign intent, not release proofFin9 by C3aLabs
THE EXPERIENCE IN ONE LINE
Priya asks: “Prepare me for tomorrow’s meeting with Mr. Sharma.”

Aura uses Priya’s role, preferences and connected information to assemble specialist work. Priya stays the advisor and decision-maker.

Evidence boundary

This report simplifies the supplied Aura experience brief and storyboard image. They describe a target experience; they do not verify what is live in production. Any client data or metrics shown in the source image are illustrative examples, not real client evidence.

01 / THE ANSWER

Aura is a chief-of-staff workflow, not a one-shot chat.

The important shift is from answering a prompt to coordinating a person-specific set of tasks, compiling sourced findings, and helping the advisor close the meeting loop.

WHAT THE DEMO SHOULD PROVE

One natural request can coordinate work that would otherwise take the advisor hours to assemble.

Show the plan, the parallel specialists, the evidence trail, and the advisor’s control. Keep Priya—not Aura—as the person the story serves.

Three things a viewer should understand

  • Personal: the brief reflects the advisor, her tools, and the client’s history.
  • Coordinated: specialist work happens in parallel, with visible progress.
  • Accountable: findings are sourced and professional decisions remain with the advisor.

The hero moment is not “look what the agent can do.” It is “Priya walks into the meeting prepared.”

02 / THE JOURNEY

Keep the story in the order the work happens.

Seven simple beats preserve the source brief’s sequence while grouping the acknowledgement and next-step offer with their natural moments.

03 / THE TEAM

Six specialists answer six different questions.

Show each output as a compact, checkable evidence card. The final brief should connect findings—not paste six unrelated paragraphs together.

01

Market intelligence

What changed in Indian markets and sectors since the last review?

Output: dated market and sector briefing with source links.
02

Portfolio intelligence

How did the client’s holdings perform against relevant benchmarks, and what drove returns?

Output: portfolio performance and return drivers from connected data.
03

Risk intelligence

What changed in concentration, volatility, drawdown exposure and risk-adjusted returns?

Output: current signals compared with the previous review.
04

Financial planning intelligence

Are stated goals on track, and did new information change the outlook?

Output: goal status and the basis for any recalculation.
05

Advisor recommendations

What should Priya discuss, and which decisions need her attention?

Output: prioritized discussion checklist—not an automatic suitability decision.
06

Meeting execution

What was discussed, what needs recording, and what should happen next?

Output: meeting notes and follow-up items staged for advisor review.
04 / THE MECHANISM

Keep the system story short and accurate.

The demo should show how context and a request become a plan, bounded parallel work, a synthesized report, and a reviewed next action.

What happens behind the experience

Short runtime path · plain-language labels

System flow
  1. Context + requestProfile, memory, connected apps and one sentence.
  2. ClassifySimple, medium or complex; this meeting-prep request is classified complex in the brief.
  3. PlanChosen model builds a dependency-aware task graph.
  4. ExecuteSpecialists run in parallel, up to five at a time, with streamed status.
  5. SynthesizeChosen model connects findings and streams the final report.

Details to reveal only when useful

  • Personal context is included in prompts: onboarding profile, memory and connected apps.
  • Planning and synthesis use the user’s chosen model; do not imply a fixed model choice.
  • The stop control is a design requirement. The source claims it cancels subagents and billing; verify before presenting that behavior as live.
  • Prompt caching is an implementation detail. Keep it out of the main demo unless cost behavior is being explained.
Primary system stepEvidence compilationStop / control path
05 / THE BRIEF

The report is the product moment.

Make the deliverable feel complete, checkable and useful at a glance. Every displayed figure should resolve to evidence.

  1. 01
    Verdict firstShort executive summary with the key conclusion and what needs attention.
  2. 02
    Evidence-backed chartsPortfolio vs benchmark, sector movement and concentration—only when source data supports them.
  3. 03
    Risk and goal signalsShow what changed, since when, and the data behind the comparison.
  4. 04
    Advisor checklistPrioritized topics and decisions to consider; never disguise them as autonomous advice.
  5. 05
    Inline citations + sourcesEach claim links to the source record; missing evidence stays visible.
  6. 06
    Export + next actionOne usable briefing, with a natural offer to draft the follow-up.
DEMO RULE

Numbers need provenance.

Use only connected, traceable figures in the live demo. If using a prepared scenario, label it “illustrative” throughout.

No decorative charts. No uncited figures. No client result implied by a mockup.
06 / CONTROL + DECISIONS

Make the approval boundary explicit.

The source storyboard describes automation after the meeting. Current C3aLabs guardrails require a human-review boundary before CRM writeback and follow-up are treated as approved actions.

KEEP VISIBLE

Advisor judgment stays with Priya.

Recommendations prepare the conversation. Priya leads the meeting, makes professional decisions, and reviews outputs before they become client-facing or recorded as final.

CONFIRM BEFORE CLAIMING

CRM updates and follow-up behavior.

The source brief says the execution agent automatically updates CRM records and files actions. The current strict guardrail says CRM updates and follow-up messages remain drafts until advisor approval. The storyboard should show a review step unless the product owner confirms a different approved flow.

07 / PREP BEFORE BUILD

Use real inputs—or label the scenario.

The supplied brief lists the missing demo inputs. Avoid inventing client-specific data to make the screen look complete.

Advisor persona

Priya’s role, firm, preferred tools, focus areas and tone. Use approved demo identity details.

PROFILE · PREFERENCES · APPS

Client scenario

Holdings, AUM, benchmark, goals and last review date. Use synthetic data unless real data is explicitly approved.

CLIENT DATA · REVIEW DATE

Evidence set

Source-backed values for market, portfolio, risk, planning and recommendations. Test examples must be visibly illustrative.

SIX OUTPUTS · CITATIONS

Experience components

Chat request, acknowledgement, task plan, agent progress, output cards, compile state and report.

VISIBLE · SPECIFIC · CHECKABLE

Meeting close

Discussion capture, advisor review, CRM draft and next-step offer. Confirm which actions can execute and which require approval.

REVIEW · APPROVAL · RECORD

Metric integrity

For each number, retain source, date, unit, denominator and status. Do not turn the example goal probabilities into client results.

SOURCE · DATE · UNIT · STATUS
08 / SOURCE IMAGE

The detailed Aura experience storyboard.

The updated image shows the desktop experience from advisor context through the briefing and follow-up. The diagrams above distill its flow in the C3aLabs system.

Details retained from the source brief
  • Six distinct specialist responsibilities; up to five subtasks can execute concurrently.
  • Personalization draws on advisor profile, memory and connected apps.
  • Planning and final synthesis use the user’s selected model.
  • All storyboard values—including portfolio returns, benchmark comparisons, goal probabilities, and allocation examples—are illustrative until backed by approved data.
  • CRM writeback is shown as reviewable pending product-owner confirmation of the actual approved workflow.
THE TAKEAWAY

Show a prepared advisor—not a performing agent.

Lead with Priya’s context and outcome. Make the plan and parallel work visible. Land on sourced evidence and an advisor-approved next step.
